title: Ecological modernization

definition.text: A school of thought arguing that the state and the market can work together to protect the environment.

facts.text: It emerged in the early 1980s among scholars at Free University and the Social Science Research Centre in Berlin, including Joseph Huber, Martin Jänicke and Udo Simonis.
Its basic assumption is that economy and ecology can be combined: productive use of natural resources and environmental media can be a source of growth, like labour and capital productivity.

Its tools include energy and resource efficiency, clean technologies, environmental management, substitution of hazardous substances and product design for environment, with radical innovations changing industrial metabolism.
It also draws on industrial symbiosis, product life-cycle assessment, and 'cradle to cradle' manufacturing as against 'cradle to grave'.
Scholars differ on whether it is only techno-industrial policy or includes cultural change, and on whether government, markets or civil society should lead; all expect innovative structural change.

Business may favour it because it meets the triple bottom line without challenging free-market principles, whereas many environmental movement views see free trade and self-regulation as part of the problem.

Critics call it greenwashing that leaves capitalism's impulses to degrade the environment intact, say it ignores environmental racism, applies mostly to Germany and the Netherlands, and rests on an impossible 'sustainable growth'.

contested_note: Its effectiveness and applicability remain a contentious area of environmental social science.
